background.definition: Ventricular tachycardia (VT) is a cardiac arrhythmia initiated within the ventricles characterized by three or more consecutive ventricular beats at a rate greater than 100 beats per minute. If the arrhythmia persists less than 30 seconds, it is considered non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (NSVT). Ventricular fibrillation (VF) is a cardiac arrhythmia during which the ventricles contract in a rapid and disorganized manner that does not allow proper blood flow from the heart. Torsades de Pointes is a polymorphic VT associated with a prolonged QT interval.

list.listitem: In US, VT/VF 1 to 2/1000 in the general medicine population; up to 30/1000 for higher risk subgroups.
Non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (NSVT) 0% to 4%; more common with increasing age and occurs equally among men and women.
Incidence of VT increases as the prevalence of coronary artery disease increases.
Although rare, primary VT/VF is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death (SCD) in patients younger than 35 years.
Ischemic heart disease (most common cause)
Non-ischemic structural heart disease (cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, myocarditis)
Non-structural heart disease (primary electrical disease, chest wall trauma)
Non-cardiac disease (pulmonary embolism, drowning, drug-induced)
The sequelae of one of the above etiologies, usually myocardial ischemia, produce areas of unidirectional block and sufficiently slow conduction in the myocardium.

Within these areas, a reentry mechanism develops during which a propagating impulse fails to die out after normal activation of the heart and persists to re-excite the heart after the refractory period has ended.
Cardiac output is reduced due to the rapid heart rate and ineffective and diminished stroke volume.
VF is generated via similar mechanisms; however, there is no uniform ventricular contraction and negligible cardiac output is generated.
ICD therapy is recommended for primary prevention in selected patients with severe LV dysfunction due to ischemic or non-ischemic cardiomyopathy.A

ICD therapy has demonstrated a survival benefit in patients with prior ventricular arrhythmias due to ischemic heart disease with either preserved or depressed LV function (occurring outside the setting of acute myocardial ischemia).A

ICD therapy is recommended for primary prevention in selected patients with severe LV dysfunction due to ischemic cardiomyopathy, those who have survived cardiac arrest, and patients post-MI with risk factors for arrhythmia.
Subcutaneous ICD devices implanted for patients with an ICD indication (but do not require pacing) are non-inferior in efficacy and appropriate therapy compared to transvenous ICDs.
In patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, dapaliflozin may prevent ventricular arrhythmias.
Patients with ventricular arrhythmias have three major therapeutic options for prevention of recurrence: anti-arrythmic drug therapy, VT ablation, and implantation of an ICD.

ICD placement has demonstrated a survival benefit in patients with ventricular arrhythmias due to ischemic heart disease with either preserved or depressed LV function. Ventricular arrhythmia in the setting of acute ischemia (such as an acute coronary syndrome) does not warrant the implantation of an ICD. The addition of antiarrhythmic drugs or ablation in certain patients may further improve quality of life.
Prophylactic catheter ablation may play some role in patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy to decrease shocks from ICD.

An RCT with 416 patients concluded that catheter ablation in patients with a history of myocardial infarction and clinically significant VT leads to fewer episodes of sustained VT below the ICD detection limit (NNT = 8) compared to medical therapy with sotalol or amiodarone.

An RCT with 1200 patients found that increasing potassium levels in patients with low-normal potassium and implantable cardiac defibrillators reduces the risk of sustained VT and hospitalization for arrhythmias (NNT = 12 over 5 years).
History of structural heart disease, especially coronary disease, in a patient with a wide-complex tachycardia, is highly suggestive of VT.C
Electrocardiography (ECG) is the standard for the diagnosis for VT and is indicated in all patients.A

Established guidelines, such as the Brugada criteria, may be used to assist in differentiating VT from a wide variety of supraventricular tachycardias (SVTs). However, if the diagnosis is unclear, wide-QRS tachycardia should be presumed to be VT.C

Differential.Differential_Features: Delta waves present, short PR interval
Prolonged QRS on comparison EKG, absence of VT criteria (fusion beats, AV dissociation, etc)

list.listitem: Several criteria for diagnosis of VT available, Brugada are most widely known (98% sensitive and 96% specific) and are listed below: Atrioventricular dissociation (more QRS complexes than P waves with no clear relationship—this is highly specific) Absence of RS complex in all precordial leads (concordance) R to S interval >100 ms in one precordial lead Morphology criteria for VT present both in precordial leads V1-2 and V6
History of structural heart disease, especially coronary disease, in a patient with a wide-complex tachycardia, is highly suggestive of VT.
Symptoms not generally useful for diagnosis but can help to establish the level of hemodynamic compromise. Transient loss of consciousness is a dramatic manifestation of VT.
Medication history is paramount since many may cause or predispose to VT (anti-arrythmics, antimicrobials, digoxin, diuretics).
Clinically detectable variations in the first heart sound and JVP (cannon A waves) are highly specific and sensitive indicators, respectively, of the diagnosis of VT.
In the unstable patient, diagnostic testing should be deferred in favor of urgent therapy.

Serum levels of magnesium and potassium and drugs levels of digoxin or other antiarrhythmics should be measured.

In survivors of VF or VT arrest who are suspected to have coronary artery disease, cardiac catherization should be considered.

Anti-arrhythmic therapy is usually not indicated for NSVT given the potential for side effects and lack of clear benefit.
Anti-arrhythmic therapy is not necessarily indicated in subjects who develop ventricular arrhythmias in the setting of acute myocardial ischemia.
In patients with cardiovascular disease, n-3 fatty acid supplementation does not prevent events (including sudden cardiac death presumed to occur as a consequence of VT).
Anti-ischemic therapy and therapy for heart failure need to be optimized in patients with ischemic disease and LV dysfunction, respectively.
Rapid access to automated external defibrillators is a central goal for by-stander directed treatment of out of hospital cardiac arrest from ventricular arrhythmias.
Boosting potassium supplementation to a goal serum potassium between 4.5-5.0 mEq/L can reduce the risk of sustained arrhythmia or hospitalization for arrhythmia in patients with ICDs.
Catheter or surgical ablation is indicated in certain patients with specific VT morphology or as adjunctive therapy in patients with an ICD receiving multiple shocks.

In patients with IHD and an ICD, a systematic review of 5 studies with 635 patients found that catheter ablation reduced ICD shocks, cardiac hospitalization, and VT storm but did not reduce overall mortality or recurrent VT/VF.

The BERLIN VT study randomized 159 patients with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator and cardiomyopathy to preventive ablation (before ICD implantation) or deferred ablation only after 3 shocks for VT. They found no benefit to the preventive ablation strategy.

Empiric amiodarone therapy has shown inconsistent survival benefit.
Patients with VT should be followed a cardiologist on a regular basis.
ICDs need to be monitored regularly for activity and battery function. ICDs can inappropriately discharge for atrial dysrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation that lead to rapid ventricular response.
In the absence of structural heart disease, VT in pregnancy may be caused by increased catecholamines.
VT can be treated with lidocaine, beta blockers, quinidine, or procainamide. Amiodarone should be avoided.
External defibrillation is warranted if the arrhythmia is life-threatening.B

cell.label: Suggestive symptoms (palpitations, syncope, chest pain) or asymptomatic
Suggestive exam (tachycardia, evidence of decreased perfusion) or witnessed arrest
Assess hemodynamic stability (vital signs, level of consciousness)
Activate emergency response teamB. Perform direct current cardioversion with appropriate sedation for monomorphic VTC and polymorphic VTB. Follow ACLS guidelines for further therapyC.

Activate emergency response teamB. Begin CPRA. If an AED is available, apply it and follow instructionsC. If VT/VF recurs after a maximally defibrillating shock (usually 360 J), give IV amiodaroneB. Evaluate and manage reversible causes and factors: volume depletion, electrolyte disturbances, drug reactions, hypoxiaC. Follow ACLS guidelines for further therapyC.
Diagnose rhythm using ECG; may be difficult to differentiate from SVTA. If unknown, presume VT in the absence of contrary evidenceC. Follow ACLS guidelines for further therapyC.
